name: Executive order of March 2, 1889 restoring the last of the Malheur Reservation (the north half of old Camp Harney) to the public domain
aka: Malheur Reservation, Camp Harney tract, restoration order of 1889
nations: Burns Paiute Tribe (Wadatika band of Northern Paiute)
promises: Not a treaty: an executive order. Royce records that the President restored to the public domain the remainder of the Malheur reservation: fractional secs. 7, 8, 17, 18 and 19, T. 22 S., R. 32 1/2 E., Willamette meridian, 317.65 acres, the north half of the old Camp Harney military reservation.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the 320-acre tract left out of the 1883 restoration was itself restored to the public domain by the executive order of March 2, 1889, that none of the Malheur Reservation lands were sold for the benefit of the Snake or Piute Indians, and that they have never been compensated for those lands.

breaches.quote: None of the lands included within the Malheur Reservation were sold for the benefit of the Snake or Piute Indians

landTaken: 317.65 acres by Royce's figure, the north half of the old Camp Harney military reservation; the Commission (Finding 37) and the 1883 order call it a tract of 320 acres.
today: Royce records that Camp Harney was excepted from the 1872 Malheur reserve and made part of the Indian reservation on July 23, 1880 (his area 647). The Indian Claims Commission's Docket 17 Finding 37 names this tract and the March 2, 1889 order and finds the Malheur lands were never sold for the Indians or paid for. The taking of the Malheur Reservation is carried by cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake, so this record is marked as the same event.

nationVoice.summary: The tribe writes that an executive order set aside 1.8 million acres for its people, dating it 1869, that the reservation was short-lived, that survivors were marched more than 300 miles to Fort Simcoe and Fort Vancouver after the Bannock War, and that the land was returned to the public domain in their absence.

The Burns Paiute page dates the executive order to 1869; Royce and the Commission date the Malheur reserve to September 12, 1872. The executive order link in treaties.json (647c.pdf) was not opened.
treaties.json lists no present-day tribes; the Burns Paiute Tribe should be listed. Not edited.
Whether the Commission's 1959 valuation of the Finding 3 tract (the reservation as bounded in 1876) included this tract was not settled; Camp Harney was added to the reservation only in 1880.

Audit 2026-11-08: Docket 17 Amended Findings of Fact (OSU id 358), Finding 37, read in full: it covers the 320 acres restored March 2, 1889 and finds the Malheur lands never sold for the Indians nor compensated. Per the coordinator's instruction the file is set broken on that finding and marked sameEventAs cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake. Royce's 317.65 acres (p. 930) and the 320 acres of the 1883 order and Finding 37 are both recorded.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. The old Camp Harney post was added to the Malheur Reservation in 1880, and its north half was the last piece of the reservation left.
plain.happened: An 1889 executive order returned those last 320 acres to the public domain. The Indian Claims Commission found the Malheur lands were never sold for the Paiute and never paid for.
plain.today: This is counted with the taking of the whole Malheur Reservation. Whether the Commission's later valuation covered this small tract was not settled.
